situation:
You are the customer relations manager and the finance and insurance manager at CASCADE AUTO GROUP, a used-vehicle dealership network formed six months ago by the merger of Ridgeline Motors and Harmon Auto. The vice president of customer experience (judge) has asked the two of you to review a recent incident involving a supplemental vehicle service agreement and to recommend how the merged company should handle a minor's signature on service paperwork going forward.

Cascade's two legacy chains never adopted the same intake procedures. Ridgeline locations require a verified adult co-signature before any customer under eighteen may sign paperwork, while Harmon locations, priding themselves on a relaxed, family-friendly buying process, have long let a teenage customer sign alongside a parent without separate verification. The service agreement itself is priced to cover routine maintenance along with the shop's cost of disposing used oil, filters and tires under state environmental rules, and the same counter check confirming who is signing doubles as the location's basic security screening for buyer identification.

The merger's public materials promised no disruption to the buying experience shoppers were used to at either chain, so any change touches an outside commitment as well as internal procedure. Last month, a parent bought a used sedan at a former Harmon store for a seventeen-year-old customer. While the parent stepped into the lobby to finish financing paperwork, the finance and insurance staff let the seventeen-year-old sign the supplemental vehicle service agreement alone, following the branch's usual practice of treating a mature teenage buyer as capable of handling that part of the transaction herself.

Combined post-merger data now show that service agreements signed without a verified adult co-signature are canceled or disputed within ninety days at more than twice the rate of properly co-signed agreements. Cascade's outside contract administrator has confirmed it will not pay a claim on an agreement it cannot verify was validly executed by an adult, and under state law a minor's signature alone leaves such a contract voidable at the family's choice.

Longtime Harmon advisors insist their informal approach has built the loyalty that keeps young customers returning for years, and warn that verifying every signature will feel like Cascade doesn't trust the families it built its reputation on. The vice president wants a recommendation on whether Cascade should require a verified adult co-signature on every service agreement a minor signs, keep each location's current practice while integration continues, or choose another path, explained in a way that protects the company from a voidable contract without costing a first-time buyer's family the welcome that brought them in.

The vice president of customer experience (judge) will greet you at the start of the meeting and ask you to share your recommendation. Be ready to explain how it reflects Cascade's core values and the factors that make a first purchase feel positive for a young customer and their family. Answer questions and provide any additional information the judge requests. The judge will thank you when your presentation and the questions that follow are complete.
judgeCharacterization: You are the vice president of customer experience at CASCADE AUTO GROUP. Business background is the same as the situation above. You have called the customer relations manager and the finance and insurance manager into your office to resolve the inconsistency in how the two legacy dealership chains handle a minor's signature on a supplemental vehicle service agreement. You want a clear recommendation for how Cascade should proceed going forward, and you want to understand how that choice will actually play out for a family walking through the door.
judgeQuestions: If we adopt your recommendation across every location, what happens the first time a service advisor has to turn away a young customer's business over a missing signature?
Once this policy takes effect everywhere, what happens if a family who was treated the old way at a Harmon store compares notes with a family treated under the new policy?
